abstract: Theobroma cacao is a strategic resource for socioeconomic development and ancestral knowledge preservation in Panama. We integrated SNP genotyping, historical analysis, and climate suitability modeling to characterize the genetic resources of Panamanian cacao and inform future conservation priorities. We genotyped 153 cacao accessions from eight provinces using 96 SNP markers, assessed genetic diversity and ancestry composition, evaluated associations between ancestry and collection habitat (farms, forests, and home gardens), and projected current and future (2050, SSP5-8.5) climatic suitability using species distribution models. Genetic diversity was moderate (He = 0.384) with high admixture (54.7%); Amelonado (46.3%) and Criollo (29.1%) predominated. Criollo ancestry was strongly associated with home gardens and, to a lesser extent, forests, relative to farms (Firth-adjusted OR = 76.8, p < 0.001, and OR = 20.7, p = 0.013), whereas Amelonado predominated in commercial farms, reflecting pre-Columbian dispersal, colonial persistence, commercial introductions, and modern breeding. Climatically suitable area is projected to increase 11.9% by 2050 (8,780 to 9,825 km2), with gains in Chiriqu&iacute, Veraguas, and northwestern Dari&eacute, and losses along the Pacific coast of Veraguas and southwestern Los Santos. Human-managed agroecosystems, particularly home gardens, play a disproportionate role in maintaining Criollo-associated ancestry in Panama, including Criollo-associated genotypes not currently held in international reference collections. We recommend a national germplasm bank and the integration of genetic and climate information into conservation and adaptation strategies for Panamanian cacao.
